items.title: DaemonSet pod can be permanently stuck Pending when its target node is saturated by equal-priority pods during mass rescheduling

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/scheduling

items.body:
### What happened?

**TL;DR:** DaemonSet pods get no priority advantage over regular pods. Since a DaemonSet pod can only ever run on the one specific node it targets, if that node fills up with equal-priority pods first, the DaemonSet pod is stuck `Pending` forever — preemption only evicts strictly *lower*-priority pods, so there is no recovery path. Reproducible deterministically in under a minute on vanilla Kubernetes (see "How can we reproduce it" below); also confirmed live on a real-world cluster after 11 days stuck with no self-healing.

After a batch of nodes were recreated (health-check driven remediation) and rejoined the cluster, a DaemonSet pod whose only eligible node (per its DaemonSet-generated node affinity) had already been filled to that node's pod capacity by pods belonging to an unrelated ReplicaSet remained `Pending` indefinitely — until an operator manually deleted another pod on that node to free capacity.

Sequence observed:

1. A node-health event caused several worker and control-plane nodes to be remediated (deleted and recreated) at roughly the same time, on a cluster topology of 3 control-plane + 5 worker nodes.
2. Pods that were running on the deleted worker nodes (from a 300-replica ReplicaSet with no `topologySpreadConstraints`) became unschedulable and queued up as Pending.
3. As replacement nodes rejoined the cluster one at a time, the scheduler bound the queued ReplicaSet pods to the first available node until it hit the kubelet's max-pods ceiling (110), before moving on to spread remaining pods across the other newly-available nodes.
4. The DaemonSet controller's pod for that same node could only ever target that one node (DaemonSet pods are scheduled via a node-specific affinity/nodeName, not floated across the cluster), but by the time it was considered, the node had no remaining pod capacity.
5. The DaemonSet pod and the ReplicaSet pods all ran at the same (default, unset) priority, so the DaemonSet pod could not trigger preemption to reclaim a slot on its required node.
6. Result: the DaemonSet pod stayed `Pending` indefinitely — not delayed, but permanently stuck, with no self-healing path — because there is no capacity-reservation or priority mechanism ensuring a DaemonSet pod can still land on its node once that node fills up with regular pods.

**Scheduler event observed on the stuck pod:**

```
Warning  FailedScheduling  (repeating)  default-scheduler
0/8 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods, 7 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity].
no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/8 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found
for incoming pod, 7 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.
```

**Only available workaround:** manually cordon the saturated node and delete one non-DaemonSet pod on it. The evicted pod reschedules elsewhere (node is cordoned); the DaemonSet pod then binds to the freed slot because DaemonSet pods tolerate `NoSchedule`. This requires manual identification of the affected node/pod per stuck DaemonSet and causes disruption to an unrelated, already-running workload — it is not a fix, and does not scale when multiple DaemonSets or many single-replica workloads are involved.


### What did you expect to happen?

A DaemonSet is a workload primitive with an implicit scheduling guarantee: exactly one pod per eligible node. That guarantee should not be silently defeated by unrelated workloads racing to fill node capacity during bulk/concurrent node-Ready events. Expected behavior is one of:

- The scheduler/kubelet admission path reserves headroom for DaemonSet pods on a node before admitting other pending pods, similar in spirit to how DaemonSet pods already bypass normal scheduling predicates for taints/tolerations; or
- DaemonSet pods are assigned a priority (or an equivalent mechanism) sufficient to preempt same/lower-priority pods on their required node when no other placement option exists for them, so they are not permanently blocked by a race they cannot participate in; or
- At minimum, this failure mode is called out as a documented limitation with a supported mitigation, rather than silently producing an unrecoverable Pending DaemonSet pod.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The original observation involved a large multi-node cluster and a mass node-remediation event, but neither is actually required to trigger the bug — that context is just *one* way a node ends up saturated by equal-priority pods. The minimal reproduction below removes all of that and triggers the same failure deterministically, in under a minute, on a 3-node [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster running vanilla, publicly-released upstream Kubernetes. No cloud provider, no CNI plugin choice, no node churn simulation needed.

**Prerequisites:** Docker and `kind` installed locally.

```bash
# 1. Create a 3-node cluster (1 control-plane + 2 workers)
cat > kind-config.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
- role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name daemonset-repro --config kind-config.yaml

# 2. Cap one worker's pod capacity low, so saturating it is cheap (real default is 110; using
#    8 here just makes the repro fast — the mechanism is identical at 110)
docker exec daemonset-repro-worker sh -c "echo 'maxPods: 8' >> /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml"
docker exec daemonset-repro-worker systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro get node daemonset-repro-worker \
  -o jsonpath='capacity.pods={.status.capacity.pods}{"\n"}'
# -> capacity.pods=8   (2 of those 8 are already taken by kube-proxy + the CNI daemonset pod)

# 3. Saturate that worker with a plain Deployment: default priority, no
#    topologySpreadConstraints, pinned to the capped node via nodeSelector so it's deterministic
#    which node fills up
cat > filler-deploy.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: filler
spec:
  replicas: 8
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: filler}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: filler}
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: daemonset-repro-worker
      tolerations:
      - operator: Exists
      containers:
      - name: pause
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
EOF
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro apply -f filler-deploy.yaml
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro describe node daemonset-repro-worker | grep "Non-terminated Pods"
# -> Non-terminated Pods:          (8 in total)      <- node is now completely full

# 4. Deploy a real DaemonSet across the cluster (no priorityClassName — same as any
#    unmodified example DaemonSet manifest)
cat > ds.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: nginx-daemonset
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: nginx-daemonset}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: nginx-daemonset}
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - operator: Exists
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
EOF
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro apply -f ds.yaml
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro get pods -o wide -l app=nginx-daemonset
```

**Actual output, captured just now:**

```
NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
nginx-daemonset-6w8q2   1/1     Running   0          10s   daemonset-repro-worker2
nginx-daemonset-hqq47   0/1     Pending   0          10s   <none>
nginx-daemonset-j7ggb   1/1     Running   0          10s   daemonset-repro-control-plane
```

The pod for the saturated worker is immediately and permanently `Pending`:

```
$ kubectl describe pod nginx-daemonset-hqq47
...
Priority:         0
...
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  21s   default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods,
  2 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity]. no new claims to deallocate, preemption:
  0/3 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod, 2 Preemption is not
  helpful for scheduling.

$ kubectl get pod nginx-daemonset-hqq47 -o jsonpath='{.spec.affinity.nodeAffinity}'
{"requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution":{"nodeSelectorTerms":[{"matchFields":
[{"key":"metadata.name","operator":"In","values":["daemonset-repro-worker"]}]}]}}

$ kubectl get pod nginx-daemonset-hqq47 filler-7d95777f96-6rxvg \
    -o jsonpath='{.spec.priority}{"\n"}{.spec.priority}{"\n"}'
0
0
```

Identical signature to the original report: node-pinned `NodeAffinity` on `metadata.name`, both pods at priority `0`, and `No preemption victims found for incoming pod`. This state does not resolve on its own — polling the pod hours later shows the same event repeating, exactly as in the 11-day-stuck pods described further below.

Kubernetes version for this run: `kindest/node:v1.36.1` (vanilla, publicly released upstream build — this repro has no dependency on any downstream distribution or unreleased version).

#### Is this ordering-dependent, or does it reproduce under a fair, simultaneous race?

The steps above deliberately create the blocking pods before the DaemonSet pod, which trivially guarantees a loss. To check whether the failure is an artifact of that ordering, we re-ran it two more ways on the same live cluster, deleting an already-`Running`, steady-state DaemonSet pod and an already-`Running` set of filler pods together, then letting both controllers race to recreate replacements for the freed capacity — the actual dynamic during a real node recovery, where nothing is deliberately sequenced.

- **Fully simultaneous deletion, no pre-existing backlog advantage:** both the DaemonSet pod and 5 filler pods on a node were force-deleted in the same command. The DaemonSet's replacement pod *won* one of the 6 freed slots and stayed `Running`. This is an honest, useful negative result: a genuinely concurrent race between freshly-created pods is probabilistic, not a guaranteed DaemonSet loss — the scheduler has no bias against DaemonSet pods specifically when everything enters the queue at the same moment.
- **Freed single slot with a pre-existing backlog (matches the original incident's actual mechanics):** with 15 filler-pod replicas already sitting `Pending` beforehand — a long-queued backlog, exactly like the 300-replica overflow in the original report — we deleted only the running DaemonSet pod, freeing exactly one slot. A backlog pod created **26 seconds before** the DaemonSet's replacement pod even existed claimed the slot instantly. The DaemonSet's new replacement was left with the identical `FailedScheduling` / `No preemption victims found for incoming pod` signature, confirmed still `Pending` 30+ seconds later.

This second variant is the faithful reproduction of the real-world trigger, and it isn't a coin flip: a DaemonSet controller can only create its replacement pod *after* it observes the old one is gone, which is necessarily later than pods that were already queued and waiting for capacity before the node came back. Against an already-waiting backlog, the DaemonSet pod is structurally late to the scheduling queue every time, not merely unlucky — which is exactly the sequence described in the original incident ("as soon as the first worker node comes back, scheduler tries to assign all the pending pods to that node... the daemonset pod remains in pending state"). The first variant shows the underlying preemption gap has no protective bias either way when pods start even; the second shows why, in the specific conditions that actually occur during a mass-remediation event, the DaemonSet pod reliably loses.


### Anything else we need to know?

### Where this happens in the code

Traced against the `v1.35.0` tag and confirmed live on `v1.36.1` (see the reproduction above). Four pieces combine to produce this failure mode; none of them is broken in isolation — each does exactly what it's documented to do — but the composition leaves DaemonSet pods with no recovery path once their one eligible node saturates.

**1. A DaemonSet pod is hard-pinned to exactly one node, with no fallback**

`pkg/controller/daemon/util/daemonset_util.go`, `ReplaceDaemonSetPodNodeNameNodeAffinity` ([L176-221](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/controller/daemon/util/daemonset_util.go#L176-L221)) rewrites the pod's `NodeAffinity` into a `RequiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` match on `metadata.name` for one specific node before the pod is created. Once that pod exists, it has exactly one place in the entire cluster it can ever bind to — if that node can't admit it, it is `Pending` with no alternative, by design.

**2. The DaemonSet controller never assigns the pod an elevated priority**

`pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go` (1472 lines in this tag) has zero references to `Priority`/`PriorityClassName` anywhere in the file — the controller copies the user's pod template verbatim and leaves priority entirely up to whatever (if anything) the DaemonSet author put in `spec.template.spec.priorityClassName`. Nothing defaults it, validates it, or nudges toward it. Contrast this with core system DaemonSets like `kube-proxy`, which only avoid this failure mode by convention — their manifests explicitly set `priorityClassName: system-node-critical`. That convention is not enforced anywhere in the DaemonSet API or controller, so any user-authored DaemonSet (including the minimal nginx one used in the repro above, and most example manifests in the docs) ships without it.

**3. With no PriorityClassName set, admission assigns priority 0 — identical to any other pod**

`plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go`, `admitPod` ([L162-172](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L162-L172)): on create, if `pod.Spec.PriorityClassName` is empty, the plugin calls `getDefaultPriority()` and stamps the result onto the pod. That resolves to `scheduling.DefaultPriorityWhenNoDefaultClassExists`, defined in `pkg/apis/scheduling/types.go` ([L24-28](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/apis/scheduling/types.go#L24-L28)) as literal `0` — unless the cluster happens to have a PriorityClass with `globalDefault: true`. A vanilla ReplicaSet pod with no priority class gets exactly the same value. By the time both pods reach the scheduler, there is nothing distinguishing the DaemonSet pod from the ReplicaSet pod.

**4. The preemption path categorically excludes equal-priority pods as victims**

`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/defaultpreemption/default_preemption.go`, `isPreemptionAllowed` ([L349-352](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/defaultpreemption/default_preemption.go#L349-L352)):

```go
func (pl *DefaultPreemption) isPreemptionAllowed(nodeInfo fwk.NodeInfo, victim fwk.PodInfo, preemptor *v1.Pod) bool {
	// The victim must have lower priority than the preemptor, in addition to any filtering implemented by IsEligiblePod
	return corev1helpers.PodPriority(victim.GetPod()) < corev1helpers.PodPriority(preemptor) && pl.IsEligiblePod(nodeInfo, victim, preemptor)
}
```

This is a strict `<`, not `<=`. Given step 3, both the DaemonSet pod and the ReplicaSet pods on the saturated node carry priority `0`, so this check evaluates `false` for every pod on that node. The scheduler reports `preemption: ... No preemption victims found for incoming pod` — exactly the event captured in this report — and there is no retry path, because nothing about the node's occupancy changes on its own once the ReplicaSet pods are `Running`.

**Putting it together:** (1) removes every fallback placement option for the DaemonSet pod. (2)-(4) remove the only mechanism — preemption — that could reclaim space once the node fills. Each function is working as documented; the gap is structural: a DaemonSet pod using a template without an explicit, elevated `priorityClassName` has no guaranteed recovery path once its one eligible node saturates with equal-or-higher-priority pods. This is why we believe the most direct fix point is (2)/(3) — either give DaemonSet pods an elevated default priority (mirroring the `system-node-critical` convention used by core system DaemonSets) so they can preempt when they have no alternative node, or add a DaemonSet-aware carve-out in `IsEligiblePod`/`isPreemptionAllowed` for a pod's uniquely-eligible node — rather than at (1) or the general scheduling-imbalance behavior tracked in #136782, since fixing spread alone would reduce how often the node saturates but would not remove the permanent-stuck outcome once it does.

### Live evidence (second, independent cluster)

In addition to the vanilla kind reproduction above, this was also confirmed on a second, independent real-world cluster — a downstream Kubernetes distribution (3 control-plane + 5 worker RHEL nodes, Antrea CNI; the original incident was observed on both Antrea and Calico clusters, so it isn't CNI-specific;) — separate from the cluster where this was first observed. Two DaemonSet pods were found stuck `Pending` for 11 days at the time of capture:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Stuck pod priority | `nginx-daemonset-2c96z` and `nginx-daemonset-nsb7r`: both `Priority: 0`, no `priorityClassName` |
| FailedScheduling event | `0/8 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods, 7 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity]. no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/8 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod, 7 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.` — repeated **3186 times over 11 days** for each pod. It never self-heals. |
| Node pin (matches code path 1) | Each pod's `nodeAffinity` is a `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` match on `metadata.name` for exactly one node — e.g. `{"matchFields":[{"key":"metadata.name","operator":"In","values":["<single-node>"]}]}`. No alternative placement exists. |
| DaemonSet template priority (matches code path 2/3) | `kubectl get ds nginx-daemonset -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.priorityClassName}'` → empty. No elevated priority requested anywhere. |
| Target node saturation | Both target nodes: `capacity.pods=110`, `allocatable.pods=110`, `describe node` confirms `Non-terminated Pods: (110 in total)` — exactly at the ceiling, not over/under. |
| Blocking pods' priority (matches code path 4) | Sampled `nginx-rs-new` replica pods occupying both saturated nodes: `priority=0` on every one checked, and the ReplicaSet template has no `priorityClassName` and no `topologySpreadConstraints`. Identical priority to the stuck DaemonSet pod → `isPreemptionAllowed`'s strict `<` check excludes them all as victims, exactly as traced in the code above. |

Two independently-stuck pods on a cluster unrelated to the one where this was first reported rules out a one-off fluke and confirms every link in the "Where this happens in the code" chain against a live, current build.

### Other notes

- This was first noticed as an apparent regression after node remediations triggered by an unrelated control-plane availability issue, but the scheduling behavior itself is version/platform-agnostic once the preconditions above are met — it is a race between DaemonSet placement and bulk regular-pod placement, not specific to any particular trigger for node churn.
- Related to [#136782](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136782), which describes the scheduler concentrating a burst of newly-schedulable pods onto the first available node rather than spreading them during a scale-up event. That issue is about scheduling *imbalance*; this issue is about the *lack of any recovery path* once a DaemonSet's sole eligible node is filled by equal-priority pods — a fix to the spreading behavior in #136782 would reduce how often this triggers, but would not eliminate it, since any single saturating event is sufficient to strand a DaemonSet pod indefinitely.
- Also related: [#54190](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/54190) ("DaemonSet controller should support preemption"), filed in 2017, which proposed essentially the same fix point identified independently here (point 2/3 above). It appears to have gone unimplemented — this report includes a concrete, current-version reproduction and code trace in case that's useful context for re-opening the discussion.
- Workaround guidance we are currently giving is to set [topologySpreadConstraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints/) on all production workloads to reduce the odds of a single node saturating. This is a mitigation on the "other" workloads, not a fix, and it is not something the platform can enforce or guarantee for arbitrary workloads, so DaemonSets remain structurally exposed to this failure mode.


### Kubernetes version

<details>
Minimal reproduction (above): `kindest/node:v1.36.1`, vanilla upstream, via kind — publicly reproducible with no dependency on any particular distribution.

Also independently observed on a downstream Kubernetes distribution in real-world use (see "Live evidence" above. 
Root cause is believed version-independent — the priority admission default and the strict "<" priority check in isPreemptionAllowed are unchanged across recent releases (confirmed by reading source at the v1.35.0 tag, and reproduced live on v1.36.1).
</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>

Minimal reproduction (above): none — plain kind (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster, no cloud provider.
</details>


### OS version

<details>
Minimal reproduction (above): whatever the kind node image ships (containerized, not relevant to this bug).

Also independently observed with RHEL worker/control-plane nodes.
</details>


### Install tools

<details>
Minimal reproduction (above): kind (Kubernetes-in-Docker).
</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>
containerd (as shipped in the kind node image).
</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>
Minimal reproduction (above): kind's default CNI — not relevant to this bug.

Also independently observed on both Antrea and Calico CNI — not CNI-specific.

</details>

items.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Since #135870 the kubelet looks its own account up with `getent passwd`. When `getent` is not on `PATH`, that lookup answers "not found" without reading `/etc/passwd`:

```go
getent, err := exec.LookPath("getent")
if err != nil {
	return false, nil // no getent: same as "not configured"
}
```

A node with a `kubelet` entry in `/etc/passwd` and a range in `/etc/subuid` then gets the default range instead. Same node, `getent` on and off `PATH`:

```
getent on PATH   firstID=1048576 rangeLen=8388608
getent off PATH  firstID=65536   rangeLen=4294901760
```

Before #135870 the kubelet was a cgo binary and `os/user` found the account through NSS, so this node used to get its configured range.

This PR falls back to `os/user` when `getent` is not on `PATH`, the shape [suggested in the review of #135870](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135870#discussion_r3966541751). `getent` stays first: without cgo, `os/user` reads only `/etc/passwd`, so an LDAP or sssd account still needs it.

Tests: `TestUserExists` checks `getent` reporting found, not found and failing, and the `os/user` fallback when `getent` is off `PATH`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #141970

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Until [#141345](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/141345) merged on 2026-09-30, a missing `getsubids` was not treated as "not installed" (`os.IsNotExist` did not match the `LookPath` error), so with this fallback a node with a local `kubelet` account and neither tool would have failed to start instead of using the default range. The hold was for that.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
kubelet: when using user namespaces with custom ranges, the kubelet now falls back to looking up the `kubelet` user in `/etc/passwd` if `getent` is not present.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

```docs

```

#### AI usage disclosure:

YES. The code and this description were drafted with an AI coding assistant. I reviewed and tested them.

/sig node

items.body:
### What happened?

A pod whose only scheduling blocker is a required podAffinity term with a namespaceSelector stays Pending with no new scheduling attempt after a cluster change that makes it schedulable:

- an assigned pod matching the term labelSelector appears in a namespace whose labels match the namespaceSelector (assigned pod add), or
- labels are added to a namespace so that an existing assigned pod now matches the namespaceSelector.

The pod is only retried by the periodic unschedulable pods sweep (`--pod-max-in-unschedulable-pods-duration`, default 5m, deprecated), and it schedules successfully on the first attempt after the sweep.

A control with the same affinity term but without namespaceSelector (matching a pod in the same namespace) is requeued and scheduled within about 10s of the matching pod being added.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod should be requeued when an assigned pod that satisfies the affinity term, including namespaceSelector evaluation, is added, consistent with the behavior for terms without namespaceSelector.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create namespaces ns-a and ns-c. ns-a has no labels initially.
2. Run pod worker in ns-a with labels app=worker.
3. Run pod scout in ns-c with this affinity:

```yaml
spec:
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: worker
        namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            team: one
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
```

scout stays Pending with FailedScheduling, for example `0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) didn't match pod affinity rules`.

4. Label the namespace: `kubectl label ns ns-a team=one`.

Expected: scout is requeued and scheduled on the worker node. Actual: no new scheduling attempt within 60s. Reproduced twice; the scheduler log shows no requeue after the namespace update.

Alternative trigger (assigned pod add): with ns-a labeled team=one from the start, create scout before worker. scout stays Pending. Then create worker. The assigned pod add event arrives (visible in the scheduler log), but scout is not requeued within 60s. Reproduced twice.

Deleting scout and recreating it schedules immediately, which shows the world is schedulable and only the event-driven retry is missing. In a longer observation the stuck pod was scheduled by the periodic sweep about 5m08s after it was parked, on the first attempt after the flush.

### Anything else we need to know?

Root cause (kubernetes/kubernetes master as of 2026-09-08, by code inspection):

- InterPodAffinity registers queueing hints only for `AssignedPod`, `TargetPod` and `Node` events. No `Namespace` event is registered, so a namespace label change cannot wake the pod.
- In `isSchedulableAfterAssignedPodChange`, the queued pod terms are matched with `podMatchesAllAffinityTerms` / `podMatchesAnyAffinityTerms` without unrolling `namespaceSelector` into `term.Namespaces`. The unrolling (`mergeAffinityTermNamespacesIfNotEmpty`) is done in the Filter and Scoring paths only. With no explicit namespaces in the term, `term.Namespaces` is empty and the `namespaceSelector` is evaluated against nil namespace labels, so the namespace half of `AffinityTerm.Matches` never succeeds and the hint returns `QueueSkip`. `podMatchesAllAffinityTerms` documents the assumption that the `NamespaceSelector` was already merged into the `Namespaces` set.
- The delete branch uses the same unmerged anti-affinity matching, so anti-affinity terms with `namespaceSelector` are likely affected for delete events as well (by code inspection, not reproduced here).

Related issues and PRs in the same family of InterPodAffinity event-driven requeue gaps: #141354 (open; pod deletion with self-affinity, plain labelSelector, different branch and term shape), #130784 (multiple required terms), #139161 (merged PR; queue hint fix for anti-affinities).

We are preparing a fix for the pod add path: unroll `namespaceSelector` before hint matching, reusing `mergeAffinityTermNamespacesIfNotEmpty`, with unit tests (the queueing hint tests currently have no `namespaceSelector` coverage), and will open a PR against master. Waking pods on namespace label changes additionally needs a `Namespace` cluster event class, which the scheduler framework does not provide today; happy to discuss whether that scope belongs in this change or a separate one. If it helps, we can also add coverage for the #141354 deletion scenario to the same test matrix.

This issue was prepared with the assistance of generative AI. All findings were verified with manual experiments on a local cluster.

items.body:
### What happened?

A `DeviceTaintRule` with the `deviceSelector` field entirely omitted (not an empty `{}` object
-- the field itself absent) makes every device on every node, across every driver and pool,
untolerated and therefore unschedulable -- not just whatever devices the taint was meant to
target.

Live-verified on a freshly-created kind cluster running v1.37.0 GA with **no non-default
feature gates set at all** (`DynamicResourceAllocation`/`DRADeviceTaints`/`DRADeviceTaintRules`
are all GA and enabled by default at this release):

1. An ordinary `ResourceClaim` targeting one device (`gpu-0`) allocates and its Pod runs, with
   zero `DeviceTaintRule`s present.
2. Apply a `DeviceTaintRule` with `taint.effect: NoSchedule` and `deviceSelector` omitted:
   ```yaml
   apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
   kind: DeviceTaintRule
   metadata:
     name: taint-no-selector
   spec:
     taint:
       key: example.com/no-selector-test
       value: "true"
       effect: NoSchedule
   ```
3. The exact same claim/Pod from step 1, recreated, now fails to schedule (`FailedScheduling`,
   `cannot allocate all claims`).
4. Also confirmed on a 4-device pool: every device becomes unschedulable, not just one --
   including a claim declaring `adminAccess: true`, which is otherwise documented to bypass
   ordinary device exclusivity but is not exempted from `DeviceTaintRule` enforcement.
5. Deleting only the `DeviceTaintRule` (no other change) immediately restores every
   previously-blocked claim to allocate successfully.



### What did you expect to happen?

According to the field's own documentation (`kubectl explain devicetaintrule.spec.deviceSelector`):

> The empty selector matches all devices. Without a selector, no devices are matches [sic].

A `DeviceTaintRule` with `deviceSelector` omitted should match **zero** devices and have no
scheduling effect -- the opposite of what actually happens.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?



1. Create a cluster running v1.37.0 (no special feature gates required).
2. Install any DRA driver advertising at least one device (repro used
   `kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver` v0.4.0).
3. Create an ordinary `ResourceClaim` + Pod referencing one device; confirm it runs.
4. Apply a `DeviceTaintRule` with any `taint` and `deviceSelector` omitted entirely.
5. Observe: any *new* claim against *any* device in the cluster -- including unrelated
   drivers/pools, and `adminAccess: true` claims -- fails to schedule.
6. Delete the `DeviceTaintRule`; confirm previously-blocked claims immediately allocate.



### Anything else we need to know?

- This appears specific to the `NoSchedule` enforcement path. Tested `NoExecute` separately: a
  `NoExecute` `DeviceTaintRule` with `deviceSelector` omitted does **not** evict an already-running
  pod on an unrelated device (its `EvictionInProgress` condition stays `reason: NotStarted`
  indefinitely) -- confirmed the eviction mechanism itself works correctly in the same environment
  via a positive control (a `NoExecute` taint with a matching selector evicted the target pod
  within 5 seconds). So the nil-selector matching bug looks confined to whatever code path
  `NoSchedule` uses to block new allocation, not the separate eviction controller.
- Distinct from #141422 / the pending fix in #141425: that issue concerns a selector that is
  *present but empty* (`deviceSelector: {}`). This report is about the field being *absent*
  entirely -- confirmed by reading #141425's diff that its new validation only rejects the
  empty-but-present case and returns immediately with no error when the selector is nil, so it
  does not cover this scenario.
- Creating a `DeviceTaintRule` is a cluster-scoped permission not granted by any built-in
  `view`/`edit`/`admin` ClusterRole -- but this bug means anyone holding that permission can
  silently take down DRA scheduling cluster-wide with one missing field, when the documented
  default behavior should be a no-op.

#### What type of PR is this?
/kind feature
/kind api-change

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR adds an opt-out path for DRA node-local preparation.

It introduces `requiresNodePreparation` as optional metadata in DRA allocation APIs and propagates it through the structured allocator and kubelet DRA manager.

When the alpha `DRANodePreparation` feature gate is enabled and an allocation result sets `requiresNodePreparation=false`, kubelet skips both `NodePrepareResources` and `NodeUnprepareResources` for that claim.

If the field is unset (or the feature gate is disabled), kubelet behavior remains unchanged.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes #137122
KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5945
KEP PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5946

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
This PR is split into three commits:
1. API + generated code + feature gate
2. Structured allocator propagation
3. Kubelet behavior + tests

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Added alpha support for DRA classes that do not need node-local prepare/unprepare calls.

With the `DRANodePreparation` feature gate enabled, `DeviceClass.spec.requiresNodePreparation` can be set to `false`, which propagates to allocation results as `requiresNodePreparation=false`. For those claims, kubelet skips `NodePrepareResources` and `NodeUnprepareResources`.

Existing behavior is preserved when the field is unset or the feature gate is disabled.
```

items.body:
## What this PR does

This PR improves the error message when CEL selectors access non-existent device attributes. When users write expressions like `device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].sharingStrategy == "runai-fractions"` without checking if the attribute exists first, they currently get a generic "no such key" error with no guidance on how to fix it.

## Why this approach

### String matching for error detection

We detect "no such key" errors using `strings.HasPrefix(err.Error(), "no such key:")` instead of `errors.Is()` because:
- cel-go's `resolutionError` type is not exported (internal package)
- The cel-go library wraps errors in `types.Err` which only forwards the error message
- Kubernetes itself uses this pattern in apiextensions-apiserver (`staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel/validation.go:759`)

### Why these three allocator files

The modification is applied to three allocator variants:
- `structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`
- `structured/internal/incubating/allocator_incubating.go`
- `structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go`

These three files represent different maturity levels of the DRA allocator implementation. They must be kept in sync because:
1. They are the core CEL selector evaluation points in DRA
2. Features rotate between them as they mature (experimental → incubating → stable)
3. Maintaining consistency ensures behavior is preserved during rotation

### Error message references documentation

The enhanced error message links to `pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/api/resource/v1#CELDeviceSelector` instead of hardcoding examples. This ensures the error guidance stays current as the CEL documentation evolves with the codebase.

### Documentation improvements

We added concrete examples to `CELDeviceSelector` showing how to handle optional attributes using `orValue()`, `has()`, and the `?` operator. These examples demonstrate the robust patterns users should adopt to avoid "no such key" errors.

## Release note

```release-note
Improved CEL error messages in Dynamic Resource Allocation to provide guidance when accessing non-existent device attributes. Error messages now link to documentation on handling optional fields using orValue() and has().
```

## Related Issue

Fixes #135661

## Test

Added unit tests in `errors_test.go` to verify error enhancement behavior.

items.body:
### What happened?

I was testing the ability to allocate both node-local resources (GPUs) along with a new network attached resource called an IMEX channel.

My setup is as follows:
* 8 nodes with 1 GPU each
* 2 pools of IMEX channels (with 10 available in each)
* IMEX channels from the first pool are part of "IMEX domain 1" and can be attached to nodes 0-3
* IMEX channels from the second pool are part of "IMEX domain 2" and can be attached to nodes 4-7

With this setup, I create two ResourceClaims, one ResourceClaim template, and 2 deployments. The two resource Claims are for two distinct IMEX channels, the ResourceClaimTemplate is for all GPUs on a given node, and the 2 deployments (of 4 replicas each) consume these claims / claimtemplates across each replica in order to simulate running 2 MPI jobs across two different IMEX domains.

Here are the specs:
```
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: imex-test1
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: shared-imex-channel0
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: channel
      deviceClassName: imex.nvidia.com
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: shared-imex-channel1
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: channel
      deviceClassName: imex.nvidia.com
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: all-node-gpus
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: all-gpus
        deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com
        allocationMode: All
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: pod0
  labels:
    app: imex-test1-pod0
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pod0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pod0
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: ctr
        image: ubuntu:22.04
        command: ["bash", "-c"]
        args: ["trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]
        resources:
          claims:
          - name: gpus
          - name: imex-channel
      resourceClaims:
      - name: gpus
        resourceClaimTemplateName: all-node-gpus
      - name: imex-channel
        resourceClaimName: shared-imex-channel0
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  namespace: imex-test1
  name: pod1
  labels:
    app: imex-test1-pod1
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pod1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pod1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: ctr
        image: ubuntu:22.04
        command: ["bash", "-c"]
        args: ["trap 'exit 0' TERM; sleep 9999 & wait"]
        resources:
          claims:
          - name: gpus
          - name: imex-channel
      resourceClaims:
      - name: gpus
        resourceClaimTemplateName: all-node-gpus
      - name: imex-channel
        resourceClaimName: shared-imex-channel1
```

When I run this, I do not get the resource allocated to each pod in each deployment as expected (instead all pods remain pending forever).

However, If I change to explicitly requesting 1 GPU from a node instead of using `allocationMode: All`, things work as expected.

One thing to note is that the code linked below doesn't consider the CEL expression selector in the `gpu.nvidia.com` and `imex.nvidia.com` device classes when calculating `requestData.numDevices`. That might be factor in this somehow:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52095a8b7b9b75d67a3882a21a6647e4f90ade48/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/allocator.go#L176-L210

### What did you expect to happen?

My expectation was that we would see 4 pods from each deployment with the following set of resources:

**deployment 0, pod0**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0

**deployment 0, pod1**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0

**deployment 0, pod2**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0

**deployment 0, pod3**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 0

**deployment 1, pod0**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1

**deployment 1, pod1**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1

**deployment 1, pod2**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1

**deployment 1, pod3**:
1 GPU from a node in the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1
IMEX channel 0 from the same IMEX domain as all other pods in deployment 1

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply the specs listed above in a cluster with the following deviceClasses and DRA resources available...

Here are my (relevant) device classes:
```
---
- apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
  kind: DeviceClass
  metadata:
    name: gpu.nvidia.com
  spec:
    selectors:
    - cel:
        expression: device.driver == 'gpu.nvidia.com' && device.attributes['gpu.nvidia.com'].type
          == 'gpu'
---
- apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
  kind: DeviceClass
    name: imex.nvidia.com
  spec:
    selectors:
    - cel:
        expression: device.driver == 'gpu.nvidia.com' && device.attributes['gpu.nvidia.com'].type
          == 'imex-channel'
```

Here is the definition of one of my GPU nodes (the others look similar except for the node name):
```
- apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1alpha3
  kind: ResourceSlice
  metadata:
    name: k8s-dra-driver-cluster-worker-gpu.nvidia.com-dpwj8
  spec:
    devices:
    - basic:
        attributes:
          architecture:
            string: Ampere
          brand:
            string: Nvidia
          cudaComputeCapability:
            version: 8.0.0
          cudaDriverVersion:
            version: 12.6.0
          driverVersion:
            version: 560.35.3
          index:
            int: 0
          minor:
            int: 7
          productName:
            string: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB
          type:
            string: gpu
          uuid:
            string: GPU-b1028956-cfa2-0990-bf4a-5da9abb51763
        capacity:
          memory: 40Gi
      name: gpu-0
    driver: gpu.nvidia.com
    nodeName: k8s-dra-driver-cluster-worker
    pool:
      generation: 0
      name: k8s-dra-driver-cluster-worker
      resourceSliceCount: 1
```

Here is the definition of my 2 IMEX channel resourceSlices:
```

    name: imex-domain-0f884867-ba2f-4294-9155-b495ff367eea-1

    devices:
```

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Device taints enable DRA drivers or admins to mark device as unusable, which prevents allocating them.
Pods may also get evicted at runtime if a device becomes unusable, depending on the severity of the taint
and whether the claim tolerates the taint.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Related-to: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5055 (initial implementation)

Based on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130120.

```release-note
DRA: Device taints enable DRA drivers or admins to mark device as unusable, which prevents allocating them. Pods may also get evicted at runtime if a device becomes unusable, depending on the severity of the taint and whether the claim tolerates the taint.
```

items.body:
The kube-scheduler is currently difficult to debug through logs. Logging is inconsistent and sparse, and critically helpful information is in some spots logged at too high of a level to be practically accessible (such as [node scores](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/b618411f1edb98afe807866fb3a607356d72ba24/pkg/scheduler/core/generic_scheduler.go#L703), which are `V(10)`. At this level logs are flooded with low-level information too quickly to even grep).

**What would you like to be added**:
Standardize scheduler logging to useful, documented levels to improve debuggability and diagnoses of scheduling anomalies. This information should be accessible at reasonable levels so as not to be flooded by irrelevant low-level process and network logs (ie, `v=2,3,4..`) and consistent across the scheduler.

Specifically, information that is necessary includes, but is not limited to:
* Filter plugins
  * Per plugin/per node
* Preemption attempts (/postfilter plugins)
* Score plugins
  * Normalized results
    * Per plugin/per node
* Nominated node result
(sub-lists to indicate potential logging hierarchies. these are just some examples)

In addition, these logs should be able to be easily traced through a scheduling cycle. That is, all logs related to a specific scheduling cycle should have a unique identifier so that relevant information can be efficiently gathered with common search tools like grep.

**Why is this needed**:
The most common issues with the scheduler are questions related to the scheduling cycle ("Why did/didn't my pod get scheduled here/there?"). While the scheduler does currently report `FailedScheduling` events, these can lack information (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91340, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91601) and do not provide any insight to successful scheduling that does not land on the expected node (eg, scoring interference).

There is demand to be able to easily debug the steps of the scheduling cycle, and the lack of that ability frequently confuses users. It would be very helpful to be able to say, "If you set `v=2`, you'll be able to see each plugin's results" for example.

/sig scheduling

items.body:
We had a micro-outage the other day when one of the machines in our cluster stopped trying to restart. On startup, it hit a transient error that prevented the server from starting up, but the pod did not try to restart again after that. The logs showed nothing between when it got stuck starting up and when I initiated a manual restart 20 minutes later. It seems we hit this issue during a network partition, though we are still investigating.

Does the pod need to talk to the master in order for a restart to be triggered?

Attached is our configuration file, including the restart policy [apiserverProdConfig.txt](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/192511/apiserverProdConfig.txt)

Thanks!

We're using Kubernetes 1.2.0

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: sig/storage

items.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:
Unable to bind a new PVC to an existing PV that already contains data from previous run (and was dynamically created using Gluster storage class).

**What you expected to happen**:
- Able bind a new PVC to an existing PV (that was created dynamically using Gluster storage class).
- Also have it documented.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
- Install a helm release which creates PVC and dynamically generated PV from GlusterStorage class (with Reclaim policy as Retain).
- Delete this helm deployment (helm del) and re-install it (helm install) making sure that we pass in  existing PV as a volume mount to the PVC instead of creating a new one using Storage class.

**Anything else we need to know?**:
I tried a few things: 
- Following the instruction here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48609. However, that did not work for GlusterFS storage solution since after I tried the needed steps, it complained: 

> MountVolume.NewMounter initialization failed for volume "pvc-dc52b290-ae86-4cb3-aad0-f2c806a23114" : endpoints "glusterfs-dynamic-dc52b290-ae86-4cb3-aad0-f2c806a23114" not found

```
  Type     Reason            Age                From                              Message
  ----     ------            ----               ----                              -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  <unknown>          default-scheduler                 error while running "VolumeBinding" filter plugin for pod "opensync-wifi-controller-opensync-mqtt-broker-fbbd69676-bmqqm": pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims
  Warning  FailedScheduling  <unknown>          default-scheduler                 error while running "VolumeBinding" filter plugin for pod "opensync-wifi-controller-opensync-mqtt-broker-fbbd69676-bmqqm": pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims
  Normal   Scheduled         <unknown>          default-scheduler                 Successfully assigned connectus/opensync-wifi-controller-opensync-mqtt-broker-fbbd69676-bmqqm to rahulk8node1-virtualbox
  Warning  FailedMount       31s (x7 over 62s)  kubelet, rahulk8node1-virtualbox  MountVolume.NewMounter initialization failed for volume "pvc-dc52b290-ae86-4cb3-aad0-f2c806a23114" : endpoints "glusterfs-dynamic-dc52b290-ae86-4cb3-aad0-f2c806a23114" not found
  Warning  FailedMount       30s (x7 over 62s)  kubelet, rahulk8node1-virtualbox  MountVolume.NewMounter initialization failed for volume "pvc-735baedf-323b-47bc-9383-952e6bc5ce3e" : endpoints "glusterfs-dynamic-735baedf-323b-47bc-9383-952e6bc5ce3e" not found
```
Apparently besides the PV, we would also need to persist `gluster-dynamic-endpoints` and `glusterfs-dynamic-service`. However, these are created in the pod namespace and since the namespace is removed as part of `helm del`, it also deletes these endpoints and svc.

I looked around other pages related to GlusterFS endpoint missing issue: https://github.com/openshift/origin/issues/6331 but that does not applies to the current version of Storage class. When I added endpoint: "heketi-storage-endpoints" to the Storage class parameters, I got the following error when creating the PVC:

```
Failed to provision volume with StorageClass "glusterfs-storage": invalid option "endpoint" for volume plugin kubernetes.io/glusterfs
```
This option was removed in 2016 - see https://github.com/gluster/gluster-kubernetes/issues/87.

@mWatney did provide a workaround solution to my Stack overflow query: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/61198972/unable-to-reuse-existing-persistent-volume-glusterfs but there is manual clean-up needed (cumbersome for a large deployment with many Persistent volume claims). So, if we can have someway to create `gluster-dynamic-endpoints` and `gluster-dynamic-services` when PVC is being re-created, that would be ideal solution akin to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/48609 but for Gluster.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): `v1.17.4`
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:  _Kubernetes cluster running on Virtual VMs created on bare metal_.
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): 
```

```

items.body:
**What happened**:
1. Created a StatefulSet with 2 replicas and 2 VolumeClaimTemplates.
2. After pods are in Running state, issue command to delete 2 PVCs attached to a pod. PVCs went to Terminating state.
3. Delete the corresponding pod. Both pod and PVCs got deleted.
4. StatefulSet recreated the pod. Pod went into Pending state and stuck there for more than an hour with following events:

```
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age                From               Message
  ----     ------            ----               ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  33m                default-scheduler  persistentvolumeclaim "nginx-logs-nginx-deployment-1" is being deleted
  Warning  FailedScheduling  4s (x26 over 33m)  default-scheduler  persistentvolumeclaim "nginx-logs-nginx-deployment-1" not found
```


**What you expected to happen**:
I was expecting it to recreate missing PVCs and bring up pod successfully.

If I delete the pod stuck in Pending state, it behaves as expected, ie., it recreates PVCs and brings up pod.
```
Events:
  Type     Reason                  Age                From                                                   Message
  ----     ------                  ----               ----                                                   -------

  Normal   SuccessfulAttachVolume  24s                attachdetach-controller                                AttachVolume.Attach succeeded for volume "pvc-3220bb3e-783f-11ea-aacd-0a6926f364ba"
  Normal   SuccessfulAttachVolume  23s                attachdetach-controller                                AttachVolume.Attach succeeded for volume "pvc-322219a2-783f-11ea-aacd-0a6926f364ba"

  Normal   Started                 7s                 kubelet, ip-192-168-182-94.us-west-2.compute.internal  Started container nginx
```

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
```

kind: StatefulSet

      - image: nginx:1.7.9
        name: nginx
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
          - mountPath: "/var/log/nginx"
            name: nginx-logs
            readOnly: false
          - mountPath: "/var/log/nginx1"
            name: nginx-logs1
            readOnly: false
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: nginx-logs
    spec:
      storageClassName: fast
      accessModes:
        - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Mi
  - metadata:
      name: nginx-logs1
    spec:
      storageClassName: fast
      accessModes:
        - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 100Mi
```

items.body:
**What happened**:
With a pod that is failing to schedule, seeing the following error:
```
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age                    From               Message
  ----     ------            ----                   ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  95s (x225 over 5h26m)  default-scheduler  0/9 nodes are available: 8 node(s) didn't have free ports for the requested pod ports.
```

This gives the information that 8 nodes failed the node ports filter, but not why the 9th node has failed. In this case, I am running a daemonset so it makes sense that there should be an existing pod on each node consuming the desired port, but my 9th pod is failing to schedule. Therefore, the information that 8 nodes don't have free ports is obvious and doesn't help debug the scheduling error at all.

**What you expected to happen**:
The number of reasons given for scheduling failures should equal the number of nodes. Is it possible that some filters are not always reporting errors when they fail?

This does not have to be an event in the pod status, but could be done through improving the scheduler's logging to make this information more accessible.

Hugepages: Pod deleting stuck

Created a pod with following configuration:

###### nginx-hugepages.yml

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx1
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx1
    image: nginx:1.7.9
    ports:
      - containerPort: 80
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /hugepages-1Gi
      name: hugepage-1gi
    resources:
      limits:
        hugepages-1Gi: 1Gi
        memory: 1Gi
      requests:
        memory: 1Gi
  volumes:
  - name: hugepage-1gi
    emptyDir:
      medium: HugePages-1Gi

```

items.body:
**What happened**:

When using K8s built on the master branch `v1.19.0-alpha.1.295+873fe1478a7984` the number of cpu's is 0 (zero);

```
# kubectl get node vm-002 -o json | jq .status.capacity
{
  "cpu": "0",
  "ephemeral-storage": "8191416Ki",
  "hugepages-2Mi": "0",
  "memory": "1531128Ki",
  "pods": "110"
}
```
Output from `kubectl describe node vm-002` [describe-node.txt](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/4432234/describe-node.txt)

**What you expected to happen**:

On `v1.18.0` and all others down to `v1.9.x` "cpu: 2" is reported, and the same is expected.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

* Install from scratch with a K8s build from master
* Make `kubectl describe node <name>`

**Anything else we need to know?**:

I install "from scratch" on a minimal system. I have missed things in the past with `cgroups` if that can be a problem this time also(?).

I build the kernel myself and have tested with (with equal result);

* linux-4.20.7
* linux-5.6

I run K8s on kvm VM's with `-smp 2` which gives 2 (virtual) cores 
[proc-cpuinfo.txt](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/4432248/proc-cpuinfo.txt)

I discovered the problem when CNI-plugins; calico, flannel and weave stopped working with
```
 Warning  FailedScheduling  <unknown>  default-scheduler  0/4 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient cpu.
```

- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):

items.title: Running second selective copy of kube-scheduler keeps assigning pods to nodes even after nodes are full

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/scheduling
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scheduling.

items.body:
**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?**:

/kind bug


**What happened**:

I'm trying to run my own unmodified copy of kube-scheduler on GKE so I can set custom policies. I've been following https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/configure-multiple-schedulers/, and trying to get things working with the default, unmodified kube-scheduler running in-cluster.

However, when my cluster gets full, my scheduler does not seem to stop scheduling pods on nodes. It should leave pods in pending - instead it assigns them to nodes anyway, where they get rejected by kubelet with `Outofmemory` (`Node didn't have enough resource: memory, requested: 1073741824, used: 10184130560, capacity: 11100332032`).

The default scheduler is still being used by kube-system, as well as the deployment running my second scheduler. Otherwise all new pods are just using the second scheduler.

**What you expected to happen**:

I expect the second scheduler to be able to schedule pods just like the default one, except with the custom policy changes I've made. I expect it to leave pods in `Pending` state when the cluster is full, potentially triggering a ClusterAutoscaler. I expect it to never schedule pods on nodes that are full.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

On GKE, here is a minimal test case:

1. lazy and otherwise dangerous service account binding (so I can rule out RBAC issues)

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: permissive-binding
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-admin
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: User
  name: admin
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: User
  name: kubelet
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Group
  name: system:serviceaccounts
```

2. Deployment running vanilla second scheduler:

```yaml
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: scheduler-2
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      component: scheduler
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        component: scheduler
    spec:
      containers:
      - command:
        - /usr/local/bin/kube-scheduler
        - --address=0.0.0.0
        - --scheduler-name=scheduler-2
        - -v=4
        image: gcr.io/google_containers/kube-scheduler-amd64:v1.9.0
        name: scheduler
```

3. A test deployment that'll fill up the cluster. Note that here I ask for 200 replicas, since that fills up my  cluster. If you have a smaller cluster, tone the number down.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 200
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      schedulerName: scheduler-2
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.7.9
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: 1Gi
```

If I remove the `schedulerName` property from podSpec, the default scheduler takes over and correct behavior is restored! 

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Environment**: 
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
  
  ```
  Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"8", GitVersion:"v1.8.2", GitCommit:"bdaeafa71f6c7c04636251031f93464384d54963", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2017-10-24T19:48:57Z", GoVersion:"go1.8.3", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
  Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"9+", GitVersion:"v1.9.2-gke.1", GitCommit:"4ce7af72d8d343ea2f7680348852db641ff573af", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2018-01-31T22:30:55Z", GoVersion:"go1.9.2b4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
  ```

  GKE

items.title: When a PVC is provisioned with delayed binding, it never recovers from a failed provision

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/storage
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Storage.

items.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!-->


**What happened**: If a PVC with delayed binding fails to provision (for example due to a StorageClass parameter error), even when the error is fixed later on, provisioning never succeeds.

**What you expected to happen**: After the error is fixed, provisioning should retry and succeed.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
- Create a StorageClass with VolumeBindingMode = WaitForFirstConsumer, and set some garbage parameters to eventually cause provisioning to fail.
- Create a PVC using the StorageClass
- Create a pod that consumes the PVC. Provisioning should fail
- Recreate the StorageClass with parameters removed.
Under correct operation, the provisioner should successfully retry and create a PV, and the pod should proceed to start. But this is not the case.

**Anything else we need to know?**:
When the PVC first fails to provision, the consumer pod has the following events:
```
  Type     Reason            Age                From               Message
  ----     ------            ----               ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  37s                default-scheduler  selectedNode annotation value "" not set to scheduled node "[node]"
  Warning  FailedScheduling  37s                default-scheduler  pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims (repeated 2 times)
  Warning  FailedScheduling  37s                default-scheduler  AssumePod failed: pod 8e98377a-fcd7-11e8-beb7-42010a800002 is in the cache, so can't be assumed
  Warning  FailedScheduling  0s (x18 over 37s)  default-scheduler  pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims (repeated 3 times)
```

after the error is fixed, the last event (unbound immediate PVCs) keeps firing.

For some reason the scheduler doesn't think the PVC uses delayed binding:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/67bc6d2083d94b38e5c8b249fe91aeafa1a0af19/pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/scheduler_binder.go#L504

One possible cause is somehow the scheduler thinks the selectedNode annotation still exists in the PVCCache (the provisioner removed the annotation after provisioning failure):
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/67bc6d2083d94b38e5c8b249fe91aeafa1a0af19/pkg/controller/volume/persistentvolume/pv_controller.go#L297
Or the scheduler failed to get the StorageClass. I'm not sure atm why either could happen.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.12.3, 1.13
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release):
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):

- Others:

/cc @msau42

items.body:
/kind bug


**What happened**:
- Scenario: 2 nodes in a cluster.
- Deployment with hostPort
- I request more instances of the given pod
- Schedules but fails to start because overlapping hostports on the node(s)

**What you expected to happen**:
Have one pod pending

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
- have let's say 2 nodes
- deploy this (or with 1 replica and scale up):
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app-name: test
  name: test
  namespace: default
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app-name: test
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 1
    type: RollingUpdate
  template:
    metadata:
      creationTimestamp: null
      labels:
        app-name: test
      name: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: <any image>
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: memcache
        resources: {}
        terminationMessagePath: /dev/termination-log
        terminationMessagePolicy: File
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5001
          hostPort: 8002
          name: nginx
          protocol: TCP
        resources: {}
        terminationMessagePath: /dev/termination-log
        terminationMessagePolicy: File
```
it will keep creating new pods which will fail into PodFitsHostPorts condition and immediately create yet another and more and more pods that fail.

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
after granting sp access to azure ACR , pull image from ACR would fail, and after wait about 15-30min(or restart kubelet directly), pull image would succeed. Root cause is that `servicePrincipalToken` needs to be refreshed when doing `registryClient.List`, otherwise it will always return empty registry list. Pull image error would be like following:
```
Events:
  Type     Reason                 Age              From                               Message
  ----     ------                 ----             ----                               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling       8m (x3 over 8m)  default-scheduler                  0/1 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu.
  Normal   Scheduled              8m               default-scheduler                  Successfully assigned nginx-server-776564f79c-zhtjk to aks-nodepool1-20881069-0
  Normal   SuccessfulMountVolume  8m               kubelet, aks-nodepool1-20881069-0  MountVolume.SetUp succeeded for volume "default-token-4t7tk"
  Normal   SuccessfulMountVolume  8m               kubelet, aks-nodepool1-20881069-0  MountVolume.SetUp succeeded for volume "pvc-5c1f0521-739f-11e8-9b69-0a58ac1f09c2"
  Warning  Failed                 8m (x5 over 8m)  kubelet, aks-nodepool1-20881069-0  Error: ImagePullBackOff
  Normal   BackOff                8m (x5 over 8m)  kubelet, aks-nodepool1-20881069-0  Back-off pulling image "andyacr.azurecr.io/nginx-server:1.0.0"
  Warning  Failed                 8m (x2 over 8m)  kubelet, aks-nodepool1-20881069-0  Error: ErrImagePull
  Warning  Failed                 8m (x2 over 8m)  kubelet, aks-nodepool1-20881069-0  Failed to pull image "andyacr.azurecr.io/nginx-server:1.0.0": rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Error response from daemon: Get https://andyacr.azurecr.io/v2/nginx-server/manifests/1.0.0: unauthorized: authentication required
```

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes** *(optional, in `fixes #<issue number>(, fixes #<issue_number>, ...)` format, will close the issue(s) when PR gets merged)*:
Fixes #65225

**Special notes for your reviewer**:
After discuss with dong, `registryClient.List` won't be necessary, instead we return `{"*.azurecr.io", "*.azurecr.cn", "*.azurecr.de", "*.azurecr.us"}` like aws, gce code logic, it will do the url matching.
I will cherry pick this PR to all supported version, every version has this issue.

**Neet to mention that** this PR would also make image pull from a cross-subscription ACR work after we grant SP access to an ACR in a different subs. Original code won’t work because it’s using the SubscriptionID of current AKS cluster, since ACR is in a different subs, registryClient.List will never get cross subs ACR repos.

```
fix issue that pull image failed from a cross-subscription Azure Container Registry
```

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

items.title: podAntiAffinity namespace defaults to all, not current as documented

labels.name: sig/scheduling

<!-- Thanks for filing an issue! Before hitting the button, please answer these questions.-->

**Is this a request for help?** (If yes, you should use our troubleshooting guide and community support channels, see http://kubernetes.io/docs/troubleshooting/.): no


**What keywords did you search in Kubernetes issues before filing this one?** (If you have found any duplicates, you should instead reply there.): podAntiAffinity namespaces

---

**Is this a BUG REPORT or FEATURE REQUEST?** (choose one): bug report

<!--
If this is a BUG REPORT, please:
  - Fill in as much of the template below as you can.  If you leave out
    information, we can't help you as well.

If this is a FEATURE REQUEST, please:
  - Describe *in detail* the feature/behavior/change you'd like to see.

In both cases, be ready for followup questions, and please respond in a timely
manner.  If we can't reproduce a bug or think a feature already exists, we
might close your issue.  If we're wrong, PLEASE feel free to reopen it and
explain why.
-->

**Kubernetes version** (use `kubectl version`): 1.6.2


**Environment**:
- **Cloud provider or hardware configuration**: GKE
- **OS** (e.g. from /etc/os-release): cos 57 build 9202.64.0
- **Kernel** (e.g. `uname -a`): 4.4.35
- **Install tools**:
- **Others**:


**What happened**:

Created two deployments with same podAntiAffinity rules in different namespaces. Did not specify `namespaces` field for affinity rules. Pods in second namespace failed to schedule due to conflicts with pods in first namespace. Had to explicitly set `namespaces` field to allow scheduling.

**What you expected to happen**:

The `namespaces` field should default to the current namespace, as [documented](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/assign-pod-node/#inter-pod-affinity-and-anti-affinity-beta-feature). Instead, it defaults to all namespaces.

**How to reproduce it** (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Consider the following deployment, which runs 2 Nginx pods that may not be scheduled onto the same node:

```yaml
apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchExpressions:
              - key: app 
                operator: In
                values: [nginx]
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

Create a cluster with 3 nodes, and apply the above manifest to two namespaces:

```sh
$ gcloud container clusters create --cluster-version 1.6.2 -m n1-standard-1 --num-nodes 3 test
$ kubectl apply -f nginx.yaml
$ kubectl create namespace other
$ kubectl -n other apply -f nginx.yaml
```

One of the pods in the second namespace will fail to be scheduled, even though the pod anti-affinity rules should only apply within the current namespace by default:

```sh
$ kubectl -n other get pods
NAME                     READY     STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-2407780625-15jkz   0/1       Pending   0          1m
nginx-2407780625-8m7h2   1/1       Running   0          1m

$ kubectl -n other describe pod nginx-2407780625-15jkz
[...]
Events:
  FirstSeen	LastSeen	Count	From			SubObjectPath	Type		Reason			Message
  ---------	--------	-----	----			-------------	--------	------			-------
  8m		15s		34	default-scheduler			Warning		FailedScheduling	No nodes are available that match all of the following predicates:: MatchInterPodAffinity (3).
```

**Anything else we need to know**:

There is an open issue for this in the documentation repo:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes.github.io/issues/2676

However, I believe this is a bug with the implementation, as the code also states that it should default to current namespace:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e443277d58e3ff1f0701ab97a1f4932389c27847/pkg/api/types.go#L1904-L1906

items.body:
The nfs example at [/examples/nfs](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.2/examples/nfs/README.md) does not work on google container engine.

The nfs-server runs but the nfs-busybox won't mount the PersistentVolumeClaim.

The busybox pod errors out trying to mount the persistent volume claim.

```
Output: mount.nfs: Connection timed out
```

The nfs-pv uses the nfs-server service ip.  Both the persistent volume and the persistent volume claim are bound.   

I did notice the nfs server logged a warning. 

```
rpcinfo: can't contact rpcbind: : RPC: Unable to receive; errno = Connection refused
```

I have tried exposing additional ports 111 tcp/udp  2049/udp but that had no effect.

items.body: ## [PHASE 1] Opaque integer resource accounting. This change provides a simple way to advertise some amount of arbitrary countable resource for a node in a Kubernetes cluster. Users can consume these resources by including them in pod specs, and the scheduler takes them into account when placing pods on nodes. See the example at the bottom of the PR description for more info. Summary of changes: - Defines opaque integer resources as any resource with prefix `pod.alpha.kubernetes.io/opaque-int-resource-`. - Prevent kubelet from overwriting capacity. - Handle opaque resources in scheduler. - Validate integer-ness of opaque int quantities in API server. - Tests for above. Feature issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/features/issues/76 Design: http://goo.gl/IoKYP1 Issues: kubernetes/kubernetes#28312 kubernetes/kubernetes#19082 Related: kubernetes/kubernetes#19080 CC @davidopp @timothysc @balajismaniam **Release note**: ``` release-note Added support for accounting opaque integer resources. Allows cluster operators to advertise new node-level resources that would be otherwise unknown to Kubernetes. Users can consume these resources in pod specs just like CPU and memory. The scheduler takes care of the resource accounting so that no more than the available amount is simultaneously allocated to pods. ``` ## Usage example ``` sh $ echo '[{"op": "add", "path": items.title: node: label persist across restart

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

items.body:
xref: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1326732 

Shutdown my labelled AWS nodes overnight to save money.   After restarting them the next morning no pods would start because they failed to match the region label selector which was set during install.   oc get nodes --show-label showed the region label missing.

The nodes were installed using the AWS private DNS name which does not change on shutdown restart.

How reproducible: Always

Steps to Reproduce:
1.  Install cluster of 4 nodes on AWS: 
   master
   router/registry  (labelled with region=infra)
   2 nodes (labelled with region=primary)

Install using the private DNS names for master and all nodes so that the hostnames will be good after restart.
1. After install set the cluster default project selector to region=primary 
2. After install set an annotation on the default namespace to use a selector of region=infra
3. Create a router and registry dc and pod - verify running on the region=infra node
4. Create some app pods, verify running on the region=primary nodes
5. Stop the nodes (not the master).  In my case it was overnight.
6. Restart the nodes, verify oc get nodes shows Ready

Actual results:
1.  All pods stuck in Pending.  kubectl get events shows FailedScheduling and failed to fit any node
2. Labeling the nodes allows containers to start.  Note:  --overwrite is not needed.   The label region does not exist at all.

Expected results:

After restart, nodes maintain their labels and do not require re-labeling.  Pods restart successfully when nodes restart 

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node

items.title: Improve clarity around PodFitsResource(issue#11453)

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

items.body:
@bprashanth @davidopp 

Related issue: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/11453

Improve clarity around PodFitsResource by showing pods limits in `kubectl describe node`

There are two suggestions in the original PR:
1. Show what resource failed in the scheduler event
2. Show each pods limits in describe node output

"1. Show what resource failed in the scheduler event" is not implemented in this PR and the reason is given below, any suggestion is welcome:)

This PR implements "2. Show each pods limits in describe node output".  The output, for example, looks like:

```
Name:           127.0.0.1
Labels:         kubernetes.io/hostname=127.0.0.1
CreationTimestamp:  Thu, 23 Jul 2015 10:37:25 +0000
Conditions:
  Type      Status  LastHeartbeatTime           LastTransitionTime          Reason                  Message
  Ready     True    Thu, 23 Jul 2015 10:59:37 +0000     Thu, 23 Jul 2015 10:37:25 +0000     kubelet is posting ready status     
Addresses:  127.0.0.1
Capacity:
 cpu:       4
 memory:    8176512Ki
 pods:      40
Version:
 Kernel Version:        3.13.0-46-generic
 OS Image:          Ubuntu precise (12.04.4 LTS)
 Container Runtime Version: docker://1.6.0
 Kubelet Version:       v1.0.0-557-g5bb5d4ee321aea-dirty
 Kube-Proxy Version:        v1.0.0-557-g5bb5d4ee321aea-dirty
ExternalID:         127.0.0.1
Pods:               (2 in total)
  Namespace         Name    CPU-limit(milliCPU) Memory-limit(bytes)
  default           apache1 1000            8000000
  default           apache2 1000            8000000
TotoalResourceLimits:
  CPU-limit(milliCPU):  2000 (50% of total)
  Memory-limit(bytes):  16000000 (0% of total)
Events:
  FirstSeen             LastSeen            Count   From            SubobjectPath   Reason      Message
  Thu, 23 Jul 2015 10:37:25 +0000   Thu, 23 Jul 2015 10:37:25 +0000 1   {kubelet 127.0.0.1}         starting    Starting kubelet.
  Thu, 23 Jul 2015 10:37:25 +0000   Thu, 23 Jul 2015 10:37:25 +0000 1   {kubelet 127.0.0.1}         NodeReady   Node 127.0.0.1 status is now: NodeReady
```

Please comment if you have any suggestions.

**Why not showing failed resource in this PR**:

I have tried to implement "1. Show what resource failed in the scheduler event", however, it seems to me that showing failed resource would require much modification in the source code. 
- The PodFitsResources verifies both CPU and Memory together in `func CheckPodsExceedingCapacity()`(https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/scheduler/algorithm/predicates/predicates.go#L118).
- The return value of `PodFitsResources` is either (`true`, nil) or (`false`, nil) after calling `func CheckPodsExceedingCapacity()`, so it is quite difficult to pass any specific resource type.
- Based on the facts above, I think specifying failed resource would result in many modifications (for instance, [1]add one more output for `PodFitsResources` and handles it OR, [2]verify CPU and Memory separately in two functions) which is a huge cost. Maybe just showing enough details in `kubectl describe node` is enough for a user to find out which resource failed for the Pod.

These are just my personal opinions, and it is quite possible that there is a good solution which I failed to find. So please feel free to share you ideas in the comments.

Regards,

Haiyang DING
